blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
blocks.content: 1. Problem Statement

blocks.text:
Every time you paste a long, messy URL into a tweet, a text message, or a slide, something quietly clever happens the moment a platform shortens it for you. A link that used to sprawl across three lines of a chat window turns into something like short.ly/a1B2c3D. Click it, and somehow you land on the exact same page as before, cookies, query parameters, tracking tags, everything intact.

That is the entire job of a URL shortener: take a long URL, hand back a short one, and make sure the short one always leads back to the right place. It sounds almost too simple to be an interesting interview question. Give it five minutes of thought, though, and it turns out to be a fantastic vehicle for talking about nearly everything that matters in system design, caching, database sharding, unique id generation at scale, the CAP theorem, all hiding behind what looks like a toy problem.

So before jumping into diagrams and database schemas, it is worth being precise about what we are actually building. We need a service that accepts a long URL and returns a short alias for it, and when anyone visits that short alias, redirects them to the original destination. Everything else, custom aliases, expiration dates, click analytics, is a refinement on top of that one core idea.

blocks.text: 2. Functional Requirements
blocks.content: 2. Functional Requirements

blocks.text: It helps to separate what this system absolutely must do from what would be a nice addition. Here is the core list, and for each one it is worth pausing on why a real product would actually want it, not just because it sounds good on a requirements slide.

blocks.text: 2.1 The must-haves
blocks.content: 2.1 The must-haves

items: Shorten a URL: given any long URL, generate a short, unique alias for it.
Redirect on visit: when someone opens the short URL, send them to the original long URL, quickly and correctly.

blocks.text: Those two alone would satisfy a bare-bones version of the product. But real URL shorteners, the ones people actually build companies around, tend to also support a handful of things users genuinely ask for.

blocks.text: 2.2 The features that make it a real product
blocks.content: 2.2 The features that make it a real product

items: Custom aliases: a marketing team does not want short.ly/xK9dP2q on a billboard, they want short.ly/summer-sale. Letting users pick their own alias (when it is available) is a small feature with an outsized effect on how usable the product feels.

Expiration: a link created for a one-day flash sale should not keep working two years later. Letting a URL carry an expiration date keeps old, forgotten links from lingering forever and quietly bloating the database.

Click analytics: nobody creates a marketing link out of curiosity alone, they want to know if it worked. A basic count of clicks, where they came from, and roughly where in the world they happened, turns this from a utility into something people pay for.
Link management: a logged-in user should be able to see every link they have created, and delete the ones they no longer want active.

blocks.text: 2.3 Rules for a custom alias
blocks.content: 2.3 Rules for a custom alias

blocks.text: Letting users pick their own alias sounds simple until you actually have to validate one. A reasonable set of rules: 3 to 20 characters, letters, numbers, and hyphens only, and run through the same blacklist filter mentioned in §26, since a custom alias is exactly the kind of thing someone might try to abuse for something offensive or misleading.

blocks.text: 3. Non-Functional Requirements
blocks.content: 3. Non-Functional Requirements

blocks.text: Functional requirements describe what the system does. Non-functional requirements describe how well it needs to do it, and for a URL shortener, these constraints end up shaping almost every architectural decision later in this document.

blocks.text: 3.1 Scalability
blocks.content: 3.1 Scalability

blocks.text: This system needs to comfortably handle billions of shortened URLs sitting in storage, and tens of thousands of redirect requests every single second at peak. That scale, more than anything else, is why a naive single-server, single-database design will not survive contact with reality.

blocks.text: 3.2 Availability
blocks.content: 3.2 Availability

blocks.text: Think about what a broken short link actually looks like to a user: they click something in an email or a text message, and instead of the page they expected, they get an error. There is no graceful way to explain that to a confused user. Because the redirect path is so exposed and so unforgiving of downtime, availability matters more here than almost anywhere else in the system.

blocks.text: 3.3 Reliability
blocks.content: 3.3 Reliability

blocks.text: Once a mapping between a short code and a long URL exists, it needs to keep existing, indefinitely, unless a user explicitly deletes it. Losing that mapping is not a performance hiccup, it is data loss, and data loss here means someone's business card, resume, or marketing campaign now points at a dead end.

blocks.text: 3.4 Performance
blocks.content: 3.4 Performance

blocks.text: A redirect should resolve in well under 100 milliseconds. Anything slower and users start to notice a hitch before the page loads, which is a strange thing to feel from what should be an invisible piece of plumbing.

blocks.text: 3.5 Fault Tolerance and Consistency
blocks.content: 3.5 Fault Tolerance and Consistency

blocks.text: When something in the system is unhealthy, cache down, one database shard slow, the system should bend, not break. A slightly stale redirect beats a hard error every time. On the flip side, the moment a short URL is created, it needs to work immediately, nobody wants to create a link and have it 404 for the first ten seconds of its life. Analytics counts, on the other hand, can lag by a few seconds without anyone noticing or caring.

blocks.text: A URL shortener that gets abused as a phishing tool or an open redirect is a URL shortener that gets blocked by every email provider and browser on the internet within a week. Security is not an afterthought here, it is closer to an existential requirement.

blocks.text: 4. Clarifying Questions
blocks.content: 4. Clarifying Questions

blocks.text: Before sketching a single box on a whiteboard, it is worth stopping to ask the interviewer a few pointed questions. This is not stalling, it is a signal that you understand how much a design can change depending on the answers.
blocks.content: Before sketching a single box on a whiteboard, it is worth stopping to ask the interviewer a few pointed questions. This is not stalling, it is a signal that you understand how much a design can change depending on the answers.

items: "What scale are we actually targeting, roughly how many new links per day, and how many redirects?" The answer decides whether a single Postgres instance is fine or whether we need to think about sharding from day one.
"Do we need custom aliases, or is auto-generated good enough?" Custom aliases mean we need an availability check at write time, which auto-generated codes never have to worry about.
"Should links expire by default, or live forever?" This changes whether we need a background cleanup job at all.
"How important is analytics, is it a headline feature or a nice-to-have?" If it is central to the product, it deserves its own dedicated pipeline rather than being bolted on later.
"Do we need user accounts, or can anyone shorten a link anonymously?" Anonymous creation is simpler but opens the door to abuse that authenticated accounts naturally limit.
"Should short codes be sequential and predictable, or effectively random?" Sequential codes are trivial to enumerate, which is usually the opposite of what you want.

blocks.content: 4.1 Why bother asking at all

blocks.text: 5. Assumptions & Constraints
blocks.content: 5. Assumptions & Constraints

blocks.text: An interviewer will rarely hand you every number you need, and that is deliberate, they want to see you make reasonable assumptions out loud and then design around them consistently. Here is what the rest of this document assumes, so every later calculation has a fixed, honest starting point.
blocks.content: An interviewer will rarely hand you every number you need, and that is deliberate, they want to see you make reasonable assumptions out loud and then design around them consistently. Here is what the rest of this document assumes, so every later calculation has a fixed, honest starting point.

items: Scale: 500 million new short URLs created per month.
Read to write ratio: roughly 100 redirects for every 1 URL created, which matches what real link-shortening services report.
Retention: links live for 5 years by default unless a user deletes them sooner.
Short code shape: 7 characters drawn from a base62 alphabet (the 26 lowercase letters, 26 uppercase letters, and 10 digits).
Custom aliases: supported, capped at a reasonable length, checked for availability at creation time.
Analytics: approximate and eventually consistent is completely fine, nobody is auditing click counts to the exact second.

blocks.text: None of these numbers are magic. They were picked to be plausible for a mid-sized, real-world link shortening product, large enough that "just use one server" clearly will not hold up, small enough that the design does not have to solve problems at the scale of, say, Twitter own link wrapper. If an interviewer hands you different numbers, the shape of this design mostly still holds, only the specific figures in §6 would need to be recalculated.

blocks.text: Start with the raw write volume. 500 million new URLs a month works out to about 500,000,000 / (30 * 24 * 3600), which lands right around 193 writes per second on average. That number alone sounds almost boring, a few hundred writes a second is not a hard problem.

blocks.text: The read side is where it gets interesting. With a 100:1 read to write ratio, we are looking at roughly 19,300 redirects per second on average. And averages hide the real danger, real traffic is bursty, so a sane design targets 3 to 5 times the average for peak capacity, which puts peak reads somewhere around 80,000 to 100,000 requests per second. That is the number that actually shapes this whole design, not the 193 writes.

blocks.text: 6.2 How much data are we storing
blocks.content: 6.2 How much data are we storing

blocks.text: Multiply it out: 500 million URLs a month, times 12 months, times a 5 year retention window, comes out to roughly 30 billion URL records sitting in storage by the time the system matures. Each record, short code, long URL, a user id, a couple of timestamps, and a flag or two, weighs in at around 500 bytes. Thirty billion times 500 bytes lands at roughly 15 terabytes over five years, before we even account for replication overhead.

The real constraint here is not raw disk space, it is spreading that write and read load across enough machines that no single one becomes a bottleneck, which is exactly the sharding conversation we get to in §18.

blocks.text: 6.3 Bandwidth and cache sizing
blocks.content: 6.3 Bandwidth and cache sizing

blocks.text: Write bandwidth is trivial: 193 writes a second at roughly 500 bytes each is about 100 KB per second, nothing to lose sleep over. Read bandwidth at 19,300 requests a second, each maybe 500 bytes of response, comes to around 10 MB per second, still modest for a redirect payload that is mostly just a URL string.

blocks.text: Cache sizing follows the classic 80/20 pattern seen across almost every caching system: a relatively small, recently-created and frequently-visited slice of URLs accounts for the vast majority of redirect traffic. At this scale, caching that hot 20% comfortably fits in tens of gigabytes of memory, well within what a single Redis cluster handles without breaking a sweat.

blocks.alt: Nodes sit at fixed points on a ring; each key belongs to the nearest node clockwise from it
blocks.caption: Nodes sit at fixed points on a ring; each key belongs to the nearest node clockwise from it

blocks.text: A naive hash-and-mod scheme, shard = hash(short_code) % number_of_shards, has one nasty property: the moment you add or remove a single shard, that modulo changes for almost every key in the system, and nearly everything has to move at once. Consistent hashing fixes exactly this. Shards sit at fixed points around a conceptual ring, and each key belongs to whichever shard is nearest to it going clockwise. Add a new shard, and it only takes over a small slice of keys from its immediate neighbor, the rest of the ring is completely undisturbed. This is the same underlying idea that powers resharding in DynamoDB and Cassandra under the hood.

blocks.text: The CAP theorem, stripped of jargon, says something fairly intuitive: when part of your system loses the ability to talk to another part, you have to pick between giving people a perfectly up-to-date answer or giving them an answer at all. You cannot always promise both.

blocks.text: 21. Security Considerations
blocks.content: 21. Security Considerations

blocks.text: A URL shortener sits in an unusually exposed position: it exists specifically to make links look trustworthy while hiding where they actually go. That is a genuinely useful feature and also exactly what a phishing campaign wants. Security here is not a checkbox, it is close to the whole game.

items: Authentication and authorization: only the account that created a link, or an admin, can delete it or see its analytics. Anonymous creation can stay open, but with much tighter rate limits.
Encryption: HTTPS everywhere, for the API and for the redirect itself.
Rate limiting: specifically on the creation endpoint, since that is the one an abuser would hammer to spin up thousands of spam links.

Malicious URL screening: every submitted long URL gets checked against known phishing and malware blacklists at creation time, and periodically rechecked, since a URL that was safe last month is not guaranteed to still be safe today.
Open redirect prevention: strict validation of the long URL format so this service itself can never be repurposed as a generic redirect gadget for someone else's phishing link.

blocks.text: If the redirect path is the most important part of this system, it should also be the most closely watched part of this system. That means four things working together, not just one dashboard.

items: Logging: structured logs on every creation and redirect, cache hit or miss included, for debugging and for auditing abuse later.
Metrics: redirect latency at p50/p95/p99, cache hit ratio, error rate, and requests per second, tracked separately for each service.

blocks.content: 22.1 What actually pages someone at 2am

blocks.text: Not every metric deserves an alert, most just deserve a dashboard. The handful that genuinely justify waking someone up are: redirect p99 latency breaching its target for more than two minutes straight, error rate on the redirect path exceeding 1%, and cache hit ratio dropping below roughly 90% unexpectedly, since that last one is often the earliest sign that something upstream (a bad deploy, a cold cache after a restart) is about to turn into a much bigger problem.

items: The id generator: implemented naively, as a single shared counter, it forces every single write in the entire system to serialize through one component. §24 covers the fix.
Hot keys: one link going viral can concentrate enormous read traffic onto a single cache key, addressed by the local-cache trick from §14.

Database write throughput: a single unsharded database has a hard ceiling on writes no matter how many read replicas sit behind it, which is exactly why §18 shards by short code instead of relying on replication alone.

blocks.alt: Two genuinely different URLs can, rarely but really, produce the same hash

blocks.text: A tempting shortcut is to skip the id generator entirely and just take an MD5 or SHA hash of the long URL, then truncate it to 7 characters. It is worth explicitly naming why this is a trap. First, hash collisions on a truncated hash are far more likely than most people intuitively expect, and now the write path needs a collision-check-and-retry loop anyway, the exact coordination cost this design was trying to avoid. Second, and more subtly, the same long URL always produces the same short code, which sounds convenient until two different users try to shorten the same URL and unexpectedly end up sharing one link and one set of analytics, quietly breaking the "my link, my clicks" expectation from §2.

blocks.text: 25. Cost Optimization
blocks.content: 25. Cost Optimization

items: Tiered storage: move old, rarely-touched analytics data (and eventually, ancient unused URL records) onto cheaper cold storage rather than premium database disks forever.
CDN caching: serving the most popular redirects straight from a CDN edge cuts both latency and origin load in one move.
Right-sized cache: the 80/20 estimate from §6 says the cache only needs to hold the genuinely hot slice of data, over-provisioning cache memory is an easy, avoidable cost to fall into.

blocks.text: 25.1 A rough sense of where the money goes
blocks.content: 25.1 A rough sense of where the money goes

blocks.text: At the scale estimated in §6, roughly 15 terabytes of storage and a cache in the tens of gigabytes, storage and cache costs are genuinely modest, typically a few thousand dollars a month on a major cloud provider, dwarfed by the cost of running enough compute to handle 100,000 requests a second at peak. That is precisely why the cache hit ratio matters so much economically, and not only for latency, every percentage point of cache misses translates directly into more database read capacity that has to be paid for around the clock.

blocks.text: 26. Edge Cases
blocks.content: 26. Edge Cases

items: A link suddenly goes viral: handled by the hot-key mitigation in §14 and the CDN caching in §25.
A custom alias is already taken: checked synchronously at creation time, failing clearly rather than silently overwriting someone else's link.
An absurdly long input URL: capped at a sane maximum (2048 characters is a common choice) with a clear validation error beyond that.

Someone visits an expired link: the redirect service checks expires_at and is_active before redirecting at all, and shows a clear "this link has expired" message instead of a confusing broken redirect.
A URL gets edited after creation: if that is even supported, it must explicitly bust the cache entry rather than hoping a TTL happens to expire soon.

blocks.text: 26.1 A few more worth naming out loud
blocks.content: 26.1 A few more worth naming out loud

items: Two people submit the exact same long URL at the same moment: both succeed independently and get different short codes, this system does not attempt to deduplicate identical long URLs, since two different users may have very different reasons for wanting their own separate link and their own separate analytics.

A short code the id generator hands out happens to spell something offensive: a small denylist filter on generated codes, checked before handing one out, quietly skips over anything on the list and generates a replacement.

The database is fully caught up but the cache still holds a stale value from just before a delete: covered already by the explicit invalidation in §14, this is precisely the scenario that pattern exists to prevent.

blocks.text: 29. Follow-Up Questions
blocks.content: 29. Follow-Up Questions

items: "What happens if one link starts getting a million redirects a second?" Point back to the hot-key mitigation in §14 and the CDN layer in §25.
"How would you stop someone from scraping every short URL in the system?" No bulk listing endpoint, and codes are randomized rather than sequential, so there is nothing predictable to enumerate.
"How would you add support for custom branded domains per customer?" A domain-to-account mapping consulted at redirect time, otherwise the flow is identical.
"How would you swap out the id generation scheme with zero downtime?" Run the old and new schemes side by side behind a feature flag, and cut traffic over gradually.

"What if two data centers each think they are the primary at the same time?" That is the split-brain scenario from the Failure Detection pattern, and it is resolved with quorum-based leader election, never by letting both sides keep accepting writes.

"How would you version the API without breaking existing integrations?" URL-based versioning (/api/v1/, then /api/v2/ alongside it), with the old version kept alive on a clearly communicated deprecation timeline.

"How would you detect and take down a link once it is reported as malicious after the fact?" A takedown endpoint flips is_active to false immediately, which is instantly visible everywhere since it is checked on every single redirect, no cache purge race condition to worry about.
